pages.c06-p01: Describe the main features of the following legislation: the Data Protection Act; the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act; and the Computer Misuse Act
pages.c06-p02: Describe the main features of the following legislation: the Data Protection Act; the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act; and the Computer Misuse Act
pages.c06-p03: Describe the main features of the following legislation: the Data Protection Act; the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act; and the Computer Misuse Act
pages.c06-p04: Understand and apply how each piece of legislation may impact on organisations, their employees and members of the public
pages.c06-p05: Explain the ethical considerations around: automated decision making; online censorship; monitoring of personal behaviour; artificial intelligence; and the capture, storage and analysis of personal information
pages.c06-p06: Explain the ethical considerations around: automated decision making; online censorship; monitoring of personal behaviour; artificial intelligence; and the capture, storage and analysis of personal information

q.q: What is the main purpose of the Data Protection Act?
o: To give the public the right to see information held by public bodies
To make it a crime to access computer material without authorisation
To protect the rights of individuals whose personal data is held by organisations
To protect the intellectual property of people who create original work
q.why: The DPA protects individuals' personal data; the CDPA protects creators and the CMA covers hacking.

q.q: Who is the data subject?
o: The organisation that decides how personal data is processed
The organisation that processes data under a contract
The regulator that enforces data protection law
The living individual whom the personal data is about
q.why: The data subject is the person the data is about.

q.q: Who is the data controller?
o: A cloud provider that processes data on someone else's behalf
The independent regulator that keeps a register of organisations
The person or organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed
The living individual whom the personal data is about
q.why: The controller decides the purposes and means of processing.

q.q: A school uses a payroll company to pay its staff under a contract. What is the payroll company?
o: A data processor
The regulator
The data controller
A data subject
q.why: A processor handles data on the controller's behalf under a contract.

q.q: Which body regulates data protection across the UK, including Northern Ireland, having replaced the ICO?
o: The Information Commission
Ofcom
The Department of Education
The Police Service of Northern Ireland
q.why: The Information Commission replaced the Information Commissioner's Office.

q.q: Collecting only the personal data an organisation actually needs is which principle?
o: Data minimisation
Accountability for harm
Accuracy of data
Purpose limitation
q.why: Data must be adequate, relevant and not excessive.

q.q: Which two laws make up UK data protection law?
o: The Data Protection Act 1998 and the Computer Misuse Act 1990
The UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018
The UK GDPR and the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
The Data Protection Act 2018 and the Human Rights Act 1998
q.why: The UK GDPR sets the main rules; the DPA 2018 sits alongside it.

q.q: Which law significantly amended UK data protection law, with its main changes in force in 2026?
o: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
The Data Protection Act 1998
The Human Rights Act 1998
The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
q.why: The notes say the DUAA's main data protection changes came into force on 5 February 2026.

q.q: A customer asks a company for a copy of all the personal data it holds about her. What is this called?
o: A right to erasure request
A data portability request
A subject access request
A rectification request
q.why: The right of access is exercised through a subject access request (SAR).

q.q: A customer asks for his old account details to be deleted because he no longer uses the service. Which right is he using?
o: Right to rectification
Right of access
Right to restrict processing
Right to erasure
q.why: The right to erasure, or right to be forgotten, applies in cases such as data no longer being needed.

q.q: A user wants to move her data from one music service to another in a machine-readable format. Which right applies?
o: Right to data portability
Right of access
Right to object
Right to be informed
q.why: Data portability lets people receive data they supplied and move it to another provider.

q.q: A person has an incorrect date of birth on their record. Which right lets them have it corrected?
o: Right to rectification
Right to data portability
Right to restrict processing
Right to erasure
q.why: Rectification corrects inaccurate data or completes incomplete data.

q.q: Against which type of processing is the right to object absolute?
o: Processing for legitimate interests
Processing to fulfil a contract
Processing for a public task
Direct marketing
q.why: The right to object is absolute for direct marketing.

q.q: Which is a right of the data subject when a significant decision is made solely by automated means?
o: A guarantee that the decision will be changed in their favour
Safeguards including human intervention and the right to contest
The right to have the organisation fined automatically
The right to see the program code used to decide
q.why: Safeguards include information, making representations, human intervention and contesting the decision.

q.q: Which principle requires that personal data is deleted or anonymised when no longer needed?
o: Data minimisation
Storage limitation
Purpose limitation
Accuracy of data
q.why: Data must not be kept longer than necessary.

q.q: Which principle means the controller must be able to show that it complies with the law?
o: Transparency of reasoning
Purpose limitation
Accountability
Integrity and confidentiality
q.why: Accountability means being able to demonstrate compliance.

q.q: Data collected for running a club must not be reused for a different, incompatible purpose. Which principle is this?
o: Accuracy of data
Purpose limitation
Data minimisation
Storage limitation
q.why: Data is collected for specified purposes only.

q.q: Which is part of the regulator's role?
o: Writing each organisation's privacy notice for its customers
Enforcing the Act and keeping a register of organisations that process personal data
Deciding why and how each organisation's personal data is processed
Processing personal data on behalf of organisations under contract
q.why: The regulator enforces the law, promotes good practice, informs the public and keeps a register.

q.q: A question asks for four principles of data protection other than accuracy. Which is the best answer?
o: Accurate; kept up to date; errors corrected; kept accurate after changes
Kept secure; kept for at least seven years; encrypted; backed up daily
Processed lawfully and fairly; specified purposes; not kept too long; kept secure
Processed lawfully; data subject; data controller; data processor
q.why: Four different principles worded as rules; do not repeat accuracy or invent time limits.

q.q: Which right means a person must be told who is processing their data, why and for how long?
o: Right to be informed
Right to object
Right of access
Right to restrict processing
q.why: The right to be informed is usually met by a privacy notice.

q.q: What does the right to restrict processing allow?
o: Having the data deleted completely from all systems
Limiting use of the data while, for example, its accuracy is checked
Moving the data to another provider in a readable format
Stopping all marketing messages for good
q.why: Restriction limits use temporarily, e.g. during an accuracy check.

q.q: Which statement about the Data Protection Act 1998 is correct according to the notes?
o: It was replaced by the Computer Misuse Act 1990
It is repealed; its ideas on subject rights and transfers are still in today's law
It only applies in Northern Ireland, not the rest of the UK
It is still in force and its eight principles replace the current seven
q.why: The old Act is repealed, but its ideas on rights and international transfers remain and are credited.

q.q: When does copyright protection begin in the UK?
o: When the © symbol is added to the work
When the work is registered with a government office
Automatically when the original work is recorded
One year after the work is first published
q.why: No registration or symbol is needed.

q.q: How long does copyright in program code generally last?
o: 25 years from publication
The author's life plus 70 years
50 years from creation
For ever
q.why: Program code is a literary work; 50 years applies to computer-generated works with no human author.

q.q: Which is NOT protected by copyright?
o: An idea for an app
The app's source code
A database the app uses
The images on the app's website
q.why: Only the expression of an idea in code or text is protected, not the idea itself.

q.q: What does the CDPA protect?
o: The personal data of living individuals held by organisations
Computer systems and data from unauthorised access by hackers
The intellectual property of people who create original work
People's right to free speech online
q.why: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects creators' intellectual property.

q.q: How are computer programs protected under the CDPA?
o: As patents
As trademarks
As literary works
As artistic works
q.why: Programs, including source code and design materials, are protected as literary works.

q.q: A school buys a single-user licence and installs the software on 30 machines. What is the legal position?
o: It is legal because the school paid for the software
It breaches the CDPA, as copies exceed the licence
It breaches the Computer Misuse Act, as access is unauthorised
It is legal because schools are exempt from licences
q.why: Installing on more machines than the licence allows is copying without permission.

q.q: What is software piracy?
o: Using open source software in a product sold for profit
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system to copy its files
Buying a site licence for every machine at one site
Copying, altering, sharing or downloading software illegally to avoid paying
q.why: Piracy is the illegal copying or sharing of software.

q.q: Which two harms of software piracy does the software industry identify?
o: Fewer jobs in shops and more online sales
Lower prices for legal buyers and more competition
Higher prices for legal buyers and less innovation
More computer viruses and slower networks
q.why: Piracy raises prices for honest buyers and software houses earn less from new products.

q.q: Which exception does the CDPA allow for a legitimate user of a program?
o: Installing the program on extra machines
Selling copies of the program to friends
Publishing a modified version as their own
Making a back-up copy of the program
q.why: Limited exceptions include a back-up copy and decompiling for interoperability.

q.q: Which licence allows free use, study, modification and redistribution under its conditions?
o: Open source
Shareware
Site licence
Single-user
q.why: Open source licences, such as the GPL, allow this under their conditions.

q.q: Which licence lets an organisation install software on every machine at one site?
o: Shareware licence
Multi-user or site licence
Freeware licence for schools
Single-user licence per site
q.why: A site licence covers a set number of machines or every machine at a site.

q.q: What is shareware?
o: Software whose code anyone may change and redistribute
Software that is free to use for ever with no conditions
Software paid for by subscription with updates included
Software free to try before payment, with the code still protected
q.why: Shareware is a free trial before payment; the code remains protected.

q.q: What does buying software actually give the purchaser?
o: The copyright in the program for 70 years
A licence to use it for one or more users
The right to copy it for friends and family
Ownership of the program and its source code
q.why: Buying software means buying a licence to use it.

q.q: What does the GPL require of anyone who changes and shares software released under it?
o: Changes must be shared under the same licence
Changes must be registered with the government
Changes must be kept secret from other users
Changes must be paid for by the next user
q.why: The GPL requires changes to be shared under the same licence.

q.q: How long does copyright last for a computer-generated work with no human author, according to the notes?
o: 10 years from publication
25 years from creation
The author's life plus 70 years
50 years from creation
q.why: Computer-generated works currently have 50 years from creation.

q.q: A student copies code from a classmate's project, changes it and publishes it as his own. Which act does the CDPA forbid here?
o: Processing personal data unfairly
Accessing a computer without permission
Adapting a work without permission
Renting out the work without permission
q.why: Modifying someone else's code and publishing it as your own is adapting a work without permission.

q.q: Launching a denial-of-service attack against a council website is an offence under which section of the Computer Misuse Act?
o: Section 3
Section 3A
Section 1
Section 2
q.why: A DoS attack is an unauthorised act intended to impair the operation of a computer.

q.q: Selling a ransomware kit on the dark web is an offence under which section of the Computer Misuse Act?
o: Section 3ZA
Section 1
Section 3A
Section 2
q.why: Section 3A covers making, supplying or obtaining tools for computer misuse.

q.q: What is the maximum sentence for an offence under section 3ZA where there is serious damage to human welfare?
o: Up to 2 years
Up to 10 years
Up to 5 years
Life imprisonment
q.why: Section 3ZA covers attacks causing serious damage, punishable by up to life.

q.q: What is the maximum penalty for unauthorised access to computer material (section 1)?
o: A fine only, with no prison sentence
Up to 10 years in prison and/or an unlimited fine
Up to 5 years in prison and/or a fine
Up to 2 years in prison and/or a fine
q.why: Section 1 carries up to 2 years.

q.q: What is the maximum penalty for unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences (section 2)?
o: Up to 10 years and/or an unlimited fine
Life imprisonment
Up to 5 years and/or a fine
Up to 2 years in prison and/or a fine
q.why: Section 2 carries up to 5 years.

q.q: What is the maximum penalty for unauthorised modification or impairment of a computer (section 3)?
o: Up to 5 years and/or a fine
Up to 2 years in prison and/or a fine
Up to 10 years and/or an unlimited fine
Life imprisonment
q.why: Section 3 carries up to 10 years.

q.q: A pupil guesses the network manager's password and logs in just to look around. Which offence is this?
o: Unauthorised access to computer material
Making tools for computer misuse
Unauthorised modification of computer material
Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences
q.why: Accessing without entitlement, even just to look, is a section 1 offence.

q.q: A hacker breaks into a bank account to transfer money to himself. Which offence is this?
o: Supplying tools for computer misuse
Unauthorised modification of computer material only
Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences
Unauthorised access to computer material only
q.why: Access in order to commit another crime, such as theft, is a section 2 offence.

q.q: Planting a virus that deletes files is which offence?
o: Unauthorised modification of computer material
Software piracy under the CDPA
Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences
Unauthorised access to computer material
q.why: Changing or deleting data or programs without authorisation is a section 3 offence.

q.q: Why was the Computer Misuse Act passed?
o: Personal data needed protecting from misuse by organisations
Software creators needed protection from piracy
Internet service providers needed powers to block content
Existing laws on theft and criminal damage did not fit hacking
q.why: Hacking did not fit existing theft and criminal damage laws.

q.q: What is the key idea behind offences under the Computer Misuse Act?
o: Payment: using software without paying for a licence
Ownership: using a computer that belongs to someone else
Consent: processing data without the subject's agreement
Authorisation: knowingly doing something you are not entitled to do
q.why: An offence is committed when someone knowingly does something to a computer they are not entitled to do.

q.q: A police officer searches a police database for personal reasons. Is this an offence under the Computer Misuse Act?
o: Yes, as authorisation covers what you may access, not just whether you can log in
Yes, but only under the Data Protection Act, not the Computer Misuse Act
No, because the officer is allowed to log in to that database at work
No, because police officers are exempt from the Computer Misuse Act
q.why: Using a system you may use for a purpose you are not allowed can still be unauthorised access.

q.q: A hacker views a company's files, then alters them, then distributes a hacking tool. How should this be treated?
o: As one offence under section 3 only
As no offence, as the files were not stolen
As one offence under section 1 only
As separate offences, each under the section that fits
q.why: The notes advise identifying each act separately: viewing, altering and supplying tools are different offences.

q.q: Which criticism of the Computer Misuse Act is given in the notes?
o: It only covers hacking, not viruses or denial-of-service attacks
It has no defence for ethical security researchers testing in good faith
It does not apply in Northern Ireland
Its maximum penalties are far too low to deter serious hackers
q.why: The CMA is criticised for having no defence for good-faith security research.

q.q: Where does the Computer Misuse Act apply?
o: In England and Wales only
Throughout the UK, including Northern Ireland
Only to government computer systems
In Great Britain but not Northern Ireland
q.why: The CMA applies throughout the UK.

q.q: A retailer's database is hacked because it never applied security patches. Which data protection principle is most clearly breached?
o: Storage limitation
Integrity and confidentiality
Accuracy of data
Purpose limitation
q.why: The organisation failed to protect the data with appropriate security.

q.q: A former employee uses an account that was never disabled to read confidential files. What is this?
o: A subject access request under data protection law
Legal, because the password still works on the system
Unauthorised access under section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act
A breach of copyright under the CDPA only
q.why: His authorisation ended when he left, even though the system still let him in.

q.q: Which step best helps an organisation make sure staff comply with the Computer Misuse Act?
o: An acceptable use policy with regular audits of computer use
Removing passwords so staff are not tempted to guess them
Buying extra software licences for every employee
Sharing one administrator account among all staff
q.why: Policy, auditing and access control help staff comply.

q.q: How does the Data Protection Act affect members of the public?
o: They gain rights over their personal data, such as seeing and correcting it
They must register with the regulator before using online services
They are responsible for keeping organisations' records accurate
They must encrypt all the emails that they send
q.why: The public are data subjects with rights.

q.q: How can an organisation help keep the personal data it holds accurate?
o: Keep all data for as long as possible in case it is needed
Use validation and verification and ask customers to check their details
Let all staff edit every record without logging changes
Share the data with other organisations to compare it
q.why: Validation, verification and regular checks by customers keep data accurate.

q.q: How can an organisation comply with the CDPA?
o: Carry out regular software audits and keep a register of licences
Buy one licence and install it on every machine
Register its software with the Information Commission
Let staff install any software they bring from home
q.why: Audits and a licence register make sure copies do not exceed licences.

q.q: An employee hacks another firm using his company's systems. When could the company be held partly liable under the Computer Misuse Act?
o: Only if the employee had been with the firm for over a year
Never, as only the employee can commit an offence
Always, whether or not it took any precautions
If it was negligent, for example with no policy or auditing
q.why: A firm that was negligent could be held partly liable.

q.q: How should usernames, passwords and access rights be used to help comply with the Computer Misuse Act?
o: So managers can share their passwords with staff
So staff never need to log in to the network
So staff can reach only what their job needs
So all staff can reach every file on the network
q.why: Access controls limit each employee to what their job requires.

q.q: What happens to an employee who misuses personal data held by their organisation?
o: Nothing, as only the organisation is responsible
They can be disciplined or prosecuted
They are automatically given a pay rise
They must become the data controller
q.why: Employees may use personal data only for their job and can be disciplined or prosecuted for misuse.

q.q: How does the CDPA affect employees?
o: They must check customers' personal data for accuracy
They may install only authorised software and must not copy without permission
They must register every document they write with the government
They may copy any software for use at home
q.why: Employees must be told the rules and must not copy software, images or text without permission.

q.q: How does the Computer Misuse Act affect members of the public?
o: They gain the right to see all personal data held about them
They must buy licences for all the software they use at home
They must report any virus they find to the Information Commission
They are protected against hacking and can be prosecuted for misuse themselves
q.why: The public are protected and are also subject to the Act.

q.q: How does the CDPA benefit members of the public who buy software legally?
o: They own the copyright in the software they buy
They are not forced to pay higher prices caused by piracy
They can see the source code of any software
They may copy the software for friends without charge
q.why: Protecting creators reduces piracy, which would raise prices for honest buyers.

q.q: An organisation suffers a serious breach of personal data. What must it do under data protection law?
o: Close down its computer systems for good
Delete all of the data that was breached
Ask each customer to pay for the investigation
Report the serious breach
q.why: Organisations must report serious breaches and face fines and prosecution if they fail.

q.q: A question asks for a step an organisation should take so employees comply with the Computer Misuse Act. Which answer would earn both marks?
o: Regular software audits, so that the number of licences is never exceeded
An acceptable use policy, which is a good idea for all organisations to have
An acceptable use policy, so each employee knows what they may access and the consequences
A firewall, so the organisation's network is protected from outside attack
q.why: Each step needs the action and its effect; software audits relate to the CDPA.

q.q: Which measure helps an organisation keep personal data secure?
o: Storing data on unencrypted memory sticks
Keeping data for longer than needed
Access levels, firewalls, encryption and backups
Sharing passwords between departments
q.why: Physical security, passwords, access levels, firewalls, encryption and backups keep data secure.

q.q: A member of the public believes a company is misusing their personal data. Where can they complain?
o: To the Information Commission
To their internet service provider
To the company's software supplier
To the Copyright Tribunal
q.why: Data subjects can complain to the regulator, the Information Commission.

q.q: Why should an organisation regularly audit which parts of its system each employee used and when?
o: To spot and investigate suspicious access
To check software licences have not expired
To decide which staff should be paid more
To measure how fast the network is running
q.why: Auditing computer use detects unauthorised access under the CMA.

q.q: Which statement about law and ethics is correct?
o: Ethics concerns what is morally right, which may differ from what is legal
Ethics only applies to doctors and lawyers, not IT staff
Ethical rules are enforced by the courts in the same way as laws
Anything that is legal is also ethical, because laws are based on ethics
q.why: Not everything legal is ethical; law often lags behind technology.

q.q: People avoid a lawful protest because they know they are being filmed. What is this an example of?
o: Online censorship
Function creep
Algorithmic bias
A chilling effect
q.why: Surveillance can change lawful behaviour.

q.q: What is algorithmic bias?
o: An algorithm that has a syntax error in its code
A computer choosing to favour its own programmer
A model trained on past decisions repeating past unfairness
A program running more slowly for some users
q.why: Biased training data produces biased automated decisions.

q.q: Which professional bodies publish codes of conduct for IT professionals?
o: The IEEE and the ISO
The ICO and Ofcom
The ITU and the W3C
BCS and the ACM
q.why: BCS and the ACM publish codes of conduct; IT professionals have no compulsory code.

q.q: Which is an example of automated decision making?
o: A bank manager reviewing a loan application in person at the branch
A website storing a customer's address for future deliveries
A customer filling in an online loan application form at home
A loan application being refused by a computer with no human involved
q.why: Computers making decisions about people without a human, e.g. loans, job shortlists.

q.q: What should an organisation acting ethically do about automated decisions?
o: Keep its decision rules secret so they cannot be challenged
Remove humans from the process entirely to avoid bias
Use any data available, however it was collected
Explain how decisions are made and offer human review
q.why: Ethical practice includes accountability, monitoring, explanation, lawful data and human review.

q.q: What is online censorship?
o: The control or suppression of what can be published or viewed online
The monitoring of employees' email, keystrokes and web browsing
The removal of a person's personal data when they request it
The collection of personal data by cookies on websites
q.why: Censorship can be done by governments, organisations, ISPs or individuals.

q.q: What is the central ethical tension in online censorship?
o: Protecting software creators versus lower software prices
Protecting people from harmful content versus freedom of expression
Faster internet speeds versus higher broadband prices
Accurate data versus storing data for longer
q.why: Most agree some content should be blocked, but blocking can violate free speech.

q.q: Which is an ethical concern about live facial recognition?
o: It cannot help the police to find missing people
It never records or stores any personal data about people
Misidentification, with error rates that can differ between groups
It can only be used inside private buildings, not public places
q.why: Facial recognition raises mass monitoring and misidentification concerns.

q.q: What is the slippery slope concern about a network manager reading staff email?
o: The same access could be misused to embarrass, discipline or blackmail someone
Staff will send fewer emails, so less work will be done overall
The manager will be prosecuted under the CDPA for copying emails
The network will slow down as more and more emails are read
q.why: Access granted for security could be used for other purposes.

q.q: Which should be in an ethical monitoring policy?
o: A rule that staff are never told they are monitored
Permission to monitor as much as possible, just in case
What is monitored and why, and how staff are informed
A rule that monitoring data is shared with advertisers
q.why: A clear, limited, transparent policy with confidential data is ethical practice.

q.q: Why does constant employee monitoring raise ethical concerns about wellbeing?
o: It causes stress and damages working relationships
It reduces the data the employer must store
It is always against the law
It removes the need for any security policy
q.why: Trust and wellbeing suffer under constant monitoring.

q.q: Which question is an ethical consideration for automated decision making?
o: Is the decision made more quickly than a human could?
Has the software been licensed correctly under the CDPA?
Is the decision based on data the person cannot control?
Is the computer making the decision behind a firewall?
q.why: Decisions based on postcode or online behaviour may be unfair to the person.

q.q: A government pressures providers to block opposition news websites. Which ethical question does this raise?
o: Whether the websites are hosted in the cloud
Whether the websites use cookies to track visitors
Who decides what is blocked, and is it simply content they dislike?
Whether the websites have the right software licences
q.why: Government pressure to block criticism raises the question of who decides.

q.q: How do cookies and online tracking raise ethical concerns?
o: They prevent advertising from funding free services
They stop people buying products online safely
They make websites slower and harder to use
People are profiled without real understanding or consent
q.why: Free services are funded by advertising, but profiling happens without real consent.

q.q: Why can an AI recruitment system be unfair even if no one intends it to be?
o: It cannot store details of past applicants
It processes applications too quickly to be fair
It cannot read the text in applicants' CVs
It learns from past decisions that may contain bias
q.why: Biased training data produces biased outcomes.

q.q: Which is an ethical concern about the analysis of personal information?
o: Producing anonymised totals to help plan services
Storing the personal data in a secure data warehouse
Profiling people to predict their health or finances without their knowledge
Encrypting the personal data while it is being analysed
q.why: Profiling can harm privacy and autonomy.

q.q: What is a black box AI model?
o: A model whose reasoning cannot easily be explained
A model stored on a secure, encrypted server
A model that has no training data at all
A model that only runs when offline
q.why: Lack of transparency is an ethical issue: a refused customer cannot be told why.

q.q: Data collected for one purpose gradually being used for others is called what?
o: Data minimisation
Function creep
Chilling effect
Algorithmic bias
q.why: The system's function creeps beyond its original purpose, e.g. contact tracing data reused.

q.q: A self-driving car is involved in a collision. Which AI ethical consideration does this most clearly raise?
o: Misuse: whether fake images could be created
Accountability: who is responsible, the developer, owner or user?
Imitation: whether people know they are dealing with a machine
Employment: whether drivers will lose their jobs
q.why: When an AI system causes harm, responsibility must be decided.

q.q: Deepfake videos raise which AI ethical consideration?
o: Transparency of reasoning
Accountability for harm
Employment and jobs
Misuse and deception
q.why: AI can generate convincing fake images, voices and text.

q.q: A chatbot poses as a human adviser. Which AI ethical consideration does this raise?
o: Bias: does the chatbot favour certain customers over others?
Imitation of humans: should people be told they are dealing with a machine?
Privacy: is the chatbot's training data kept confidential?
Employment: should the human adviser have kept their job?
q.why: People may need to be told when they are dealing with a machine.

q.q: AI image models trained on photos scraped from social media raise which concern?
o: Privacy, as personal data is used without clear consent
Accountability, as the photos are owned by the AI
Employment, as photographers will be paid more
Transparency, as the photos are too small to see
q.why: AI is often trained on personal data collected without clear consent.

q.q: Which ethical question belongs to the capture stage of personal information?
o: Who inside the organisation can see the stored data?
Is the data combined so people can be re-identified?
Is the data sold to other organisations?
Have people genuinely consented, or just clicked accept?
q.why: Capture questions are about awareness and consent; the others belong to storage, analysis and sharing.

q.q: Which ethical question belongs to the storage stage of personal information?
o: Is the data kept securely and for no longer than needed?
Do people know what is being collected by apps?
Is the data passed to organisations the person never imagined?
Is the data used to set different prices for different people?
q.why: Storage questions concern security, retention and access.

q.q: The right to private life is set out in Article 8 of which document?
o: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
The European Convention on Human Rights
The UK GDPR
q.why: Article 8 of the ECHR, given effect in the UK by the Human Rights Act 1998.

q.q: Which phrase sums up the security side of the security versus privacy debate?
o: The right to be forgotten
Nothing to hide, nothing to fear
Innocent until proven guilty
Privacy by design and default
q.why: This argument is set against the right to private life.

q.q: Employers and the state hold far more power than the individuals they monitor. Which ethical consideration is this?
o: Function creep
Power imbalance
Chilling effect
Accuracy and bias
q.why: The notes list power imbalance as an ethical consideration of monitoring.

q.q: A 9-mark question asks about the ethics of companies using personal information. How should the answer be organised, according to the notes?
o: A list of advantages for the company, then a list of advantages for customers
Capture and storage only, with a definition and example of each term
Each relevant law in turn, with its penalties and the regulator's powers
Capture, storage, analysis and sharing, with a benefit and concern at each, then a judgement
q.why: The notes advise capture, storage, analysis, sharing, then a reasoned judgement.

q.q: Which is an ethical question about the ownership of digital content?
o: Should the song be stored as a compressed file to save space?
If a friend copies a song they bought, who is paid and who should profit?
Was the song file encrypted when it was shared with the friend?
Can the song be stored in a data warehouse for later analysis?
q.why: The creator is not paid when copies are shared, raising questions of ownership.
